title: Antifungal drugs for invasive fungal infections
subject: subj:infectious

provenance.note: M3 Antifungal drugs for IFI (2026).pdf (Infectious Diseases, Pr. Ahd Oulad Lahsen)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Four classes: polyenes, azoles, echinocandins, 5-flucytosine.
Amphotericin binds ergosterol; azoles block its synthesis; echinocandins block β-D-glucan.
Amphotericin B: broad, fungicidal, IV only; nephrotoxic, ↓K ↓Mg; lipid forms safer.
5-FC: always combined (cryptococcosis); marrow toxicity.
Fluconazole: Candida + Cryptococcus, not Aspergillus or C. krusei.
Mucorales: amphotericin, posaconazole, isavuconazole.
Azoles: interactions, loading dose, hepatotoxicity, QT (not isavuconazole).
Voriconazole: visual hallucinations, photosensitivity, skin cancer.
Echinocandins: IV, poor CSF/urine, not Cryptococcus; few interactions.

deeper.title: Why antifungals are harder to design than antibiotics
deeper.html:
Fungi are eukaryotes like us: their ribosomes, nuclei and metabolism resemble human ones, so few targets are truly unique. The main exploitable differences are ergosterol instead of cholesterol in the membrane and a β-glucan cell wall, which is exactly what the four classes attack. Even so, amphotericin binds cholesterol a little, which explains its kidney toxicity.

Source: the lecture's mechanism slide.

deeper.title: Why echinocandins fail in cryptococcal meningitis
deeper.html:
Cryptococcus has little β-glucan in its wall, so echinocandins barely affect it, and these large molecules also penetrate poorly into the cerebrospinal fluid. Cryptococcal meningitis is therefore treated with amphotericin B plus flucytosine, which reach the CSF and act on the organism.

Source: the lecture's echinocandin and 5-FC slides.

figure.caption: Four classes, four fungal structures. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Toxicity: ampho → kidney; azoles → liver, QT

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Acyclovir: HSV ≫ VZV; phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase.
Valaciclovir gives 3× acyclovir levels; very active on VZV.
Famciclovir = prodrug of penciclovir.
Ganciclovir/valganciclovir: CMV; myelotoxic; not if neutrophils < 500.
Foscarnet: nephrotoxic, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, genital ulcers.
Cidofovir: t½ 65 h, spaced dosing, with probenecid; nephrotoxic, uveitis.
HBV first line: tenofovir.
HCV: -previr (protease), -asvir (NS5A), -buvir (polymerase); sofosbuvir.
NRTI: chain termination; NNRTI: allosteric, low genetic barrier.
ARV classes: NRTI, NNRTI, PI, integrase inhibitors (+ entry inhibitors).
Oseltamivir within 48 h; amantadine obsolete (resistance).

deeper.title: Why acyclovir spares healthy cells
deeper.html:
Acyclovir is harmless until it is phosphorylated, and the first phosphate is added efficiently only by the thymidine kinase that herpes simplex encodes. Uninfected cells barely activate it, so the drug concentrates as a triphosphate inside infected cells, where it blocks the viral DNA polymerase. Viruses that lose or change their thymidine kinase become resistant, and then foscarnet, which needs no activation, is used.

Source: the lecture's anti-herpesviridae mechanism diagram.

deeper.title: Why HIV is treated with several drug classes
deeper.html:
HIV's reverse transcriptase makes many errors, so resistant variants arise constantly. A single drug, especially an NNRTI with a low genetic barrier, is quickly defeated by one mutation. Combining drugs from different classes means a virus would need several independent mutations at once, which keeps it suppressed.

Source: the lecture's antiretroviral classes slides.

labels: HIV: NRTI, NNRTI, PI, integrase, entry

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Antibiotics treat bacterial infections only; no antibiotics for colds.
Goals: efficacy, tolerance, minimum cost.
Bactericidal: < 1 survivor per 100,000; bacteriostatic relies on immunity.
Time-dependent (T > MIC): β-lactams, vancomycin, macrolides → divide doses.
Concentration-dependent (peak/MIC): aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones → once daily.
Choose by germ, site, resistance, host.
UTI empiric target: Gram-negative bacilli.
Intracellular germs: Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Legionella.
Multiresistant: Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter.
Pregnancy: avoid cyclins, aminoglycosides, quinolones, high-dose metronidazole.
Combine for endocarditis, listeriosis, brucellosis, TB, polymicrobial and critically ill.
Response: fever, CRP, white count, cultures.

deeper.title: Why dosing schedule depends on how the drug kills
deeper.html:
β-lactams kill only while bacteria are exposed above the MIC; a huge peak adds nothing, but a gap below the MIC lets bacteria regrow. Aminoglycosides kill faster the higher the peak and keep suppressing growth after levels fall (post-antibiotic effect). So the same daily amount is best split for a β-lactam but given at once for an aminoglycoside, which also reduces its kidney and ear toxicity.

Source: the lecture's pharmacodynamic principle slides.

deeper.title: Why combinations prevent resistance in tuberculosis
deeper.html:
In a large bacterial population, a few organisms already carry a random mutation resisting any single drug. One drug selects them; two or more drugs with different targets make it vanishingly unlikely that one bacterium resists all at once. That is why TB is always treated with a combination.

Source: the lecture's combination slide.

figure.caption: The four questions behind every prescription. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: The site: tissue and intracellular diffusion
The host: age, pregnancy, kidney, liver, allergy

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Vibrio cholerae: Gram-negative comma rod, polar flagellum.
Notifiable disease; epidemics where water and sanitation fail.
Cholera toxin → secretory diarrhoea up to 15 L/day.
Faecal-oral: contaminated water and food.
Incubation hours to 5 days.
Rice-water stools, afebrile, vomiting, cramps.
Risks: hypovolaemic shock, acute renal failure.
Confirm with stool culture on TCBS.
Rehydration is the cornerstone: ORS, Ringer lactate.
Doxycycline single dose first line; azithromycin in children.
Oral inactivated vaccines: Dukoral, Shanchol, Euvichol.

deeper.title: Why oral rehydration works despite ongoing diarrhoea
deeper.html:
Cholera toxin disables the gut's normal salt absorption, but the sodium-glucose co-transporter still works. Oral rehydration salts contain glucose and sodium together, which are absorbed through that pathway and pull water with them. Replacing losses this way keeps most patients alive without a drip, which is why ORS is the cornerstone of treatment.

Source: the lecture's treatment slide.

deeper.title: Why cholera follows disasters and wars
deeper.html:
Cholera spreads when faeces contaminate drinking water. Floods, earthquakes and conflicts destroy water systems and sanitation and crowd people together, so a single case can seed a large outbreak within days. Clean water and sanitation prevent it far more than any drug.

Source: the lecture's transmission and epidemiology slide.

figure.caption: From contaminated water to shock, and how to stop it. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Rice-water stools, up to 15 L/day, afebrile

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: HIV: chronic, no cure, no vaccine, lifelong ART, near-normal life expectancy with treatment.
HIV-1 worldwide; HIV-2 West Africa.
Target: CD4+ T cells (90% of infected cells).
Morocco: prevalence ~0.08%, concentrated in key populations, mainly heterosexual.
PrEP: TDF/FTC daily, until 2 days after last exposure.
PEP: triple therapy within 4 h (max 48-72 h) for 4 weeks.
Mother-to-child: 25-40% untreated → < 1% with ARVs and no breastfeeding.
Screening: 4th-generation ELISA (Ab + p24) or rapid test; confirm with viral load.
5 Cs of testing: consent, counselling, confidentiality, correct results, connection to care.
CD4 < 200: Pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis; < 100: cryptococcus, CMV, MAC.
ART: 2 NRTIs + NNRTI or PI or integrase inhibitor, for life.

deeper.title: Why an undetectable viral load protects partners
deeper.html:
Transmission depends on how much virus is present in blood and genital fluids. When ART keeps the viral load undetectable, there is too little virus to infect a partner, so treatment is itself prevention. That is why the lecture lists 'reduce HIV transmission' among the goals of ART, not just individual health.

Source: the lecture's objectives of ARV treatment slide.

deeper.title: Why the CD4 count predicts which infection appears
deeper.html:
Different pathogens need different degrees of immune failure to cause disease. Tuberculosis and candidiasis can break through a mildly weakened system, while Pneumocystis, toxoplasmosis and then CMV and cryptococcus only emerge when CD4 cells fall very low. The count therefore tells you what to look for and when to start preventive treatment.

Source: the lecture's CD4 and clinical manifestations slide.

figure.caption: The lower the CD4 count, the more severe the infections. Schematic drawn for this site.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Oesophageal candidiasis: dysphagia, retrosternal pain, white coating → endoscopy, fluconazole, HIV test.
TB: commonest OI, all CD4 levels, ~1/3 of HIV deaths.
HIV ↑ TB risk (↓ Th1, IFN-γ); TB ↑ HIV replication (TNF, IL-1, IL-6).
Every TB → HIV test; every HIV → TB assessment.
CMV: CD4 < 50; retinitis → blindness.
Cryptosporidiosis: chronic diarrhoea, sclerosing cholangitis.
Kaposi = HHV-8; lymphoma = EBV; cervical cancer = HPV.
Kaposi lesions: purple-brown macules and nodules; biopsy.

deeper.title: Why TB and HIV make each other worse
deeper.html:
Controlling TB depends on Th1 cells that release interferon-γ to activate macrophages; HIV destroys exactly those cells, so latent TB reactivates. In turn, the inflammation of active TB floods tissues with TNF and interleukins that switch on HIV replication in infected cells. Each disease speeds the other, which is why they are always screened for together.

Source: the lecture's tuberculosis slides.

deeper.title: Why these cancers are called AIDS-defining
deeper.html:
Kaposi sarcoma, EBV lymphomas and HPV cervical cancer are caused by viruses the immune system normally keeps in check. When HIV removes that surveillance, the viruses drive malignant growth. Finding one of these cancers therefore suggests severe immunosuppression and should always trigger an HIV test.

Source: the lecture's cancers slide.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Leptospirosis: zoonosis due to Leptospira interrogans.
Morocco: L. icterohaemorrhagiae most common.
Reservoir: rodents, dogs, pigs; urine in water/soil.
Entry: cuts, mucosa, conjunctiva; sewer workers, slaughterhouses, miners.
Anicteric: flu-like, self-limited; immune stage with aseptic meningitis.
Icteric: fever, jaundice, renal failure, haemorrhage.
PCR from day 1; ELISA IgM day 8; MAT (reference) day 10.
Serology: two samples 15 days apart.
Penicillin/amoxicillin 10 d, ceftriaxone 7-10 d or doxycycline 7 d.
Dialysis and resuscitation often needed.
Prevention: rodent control, bathing hygiene, protection, vaccine for workers.

deeper.title: Why PCR, not serology, is used in the first week
deeper.html:
Antibodies take about a week to appear: ELISA IgM from day 8 and MAT from day 10. In the first days the bacteria are circulating in the blood, so PCR can detect their DNA from day 1. A negative serology early in the illness therefore does not exclude leptospirosis, which is why a second sample two weeks later is needed.

Source: the lecture's biological diagnosis slide.

deeper.title: Why the kidney is hit so hard
deeper.html:
Leptospires colonise the renal tubules, which is also how infected animals keep shedding them in urine. In humans this causes tubular and interstitial damage, and combined with dehydration and haemorrhage leads to acute renal failure, one of the main causes of death in the icteric form.

Source: the lecture's icteric syndrome and treatment slides.

figure.caption: A zoonosis from rodent urine to jaundice and renal failure. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Rodents, dogs, pigs: urine in water/soil
Icteric (Weil): fever, jaundice, renal failure, haemorrhage
PCR from D1; MAT (reference) from D10; ELISA IgM D8

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Meningitis is a medical emergency.
Adults: meningococcus, pneumococcus, TB. Newborns: GBS, E. coli, Listeria.
Meningeal syndrome: headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, photophobia + fever.
Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Severity: extensive purpura, deficit, coma, shock.
LP must never delay antibiotics.
LP contraindications: skin sepsis, coagulopathy, raised ICP, mass.
Purulent: ≥ 1,000 cells, PMN, glucose ↓. Viral: < 100 lymphocytes, glucose normal.
TB: progressive, oculomotor palsy, protein > 1 g/L, glucose ↓, hyponatraemia.
Listeria: pregnancy, alcohol, immunosuppression; cranial nerve palsies.
Ceftriaxone/cefotaxime; 7 d meningococcus, 10-14 d pneumococcus.
Listeria: amoxicillin + gentamicin.
Contacts: rifampicin 600 mg × 2/day for 2 days.

deeper.title: Why antibiotics come before the lumbar puncture if needed
deeper.html:
Bacterial meningitis can kill within hours, and every hour of delay worsens outcome. If a CT is needed first because of signs of raised pressure, waiting for the scan and the tap could cost the patient their life. Blood cultures are taken and antibiotics started at once; the CSF can still show cells and antigens even after the first dose.

Source: the lecture's lumbar puncture slide.

deeper.title: Why a clear lymphocytic CSF with low glucose is a warning
deeper.html:
Viral meningitis usually leaves glucose normal. When lymphocytes dominate but glucose is low, think of tuberculosis, Listeria or a bacterial meningitis already partly treated by antibiotics. These need specific, prolonged treatment, so this CSF pattern should never be dismissed as 'just viral'.

Source: the lecture's CSF interpretation slide.

figure.caption: Appearance and cells point to the cause. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Clear, lymphocytes, glucose ↓: TB, Listeria, decapitated

provenance.note: 20 WS Prolonged fever.pdf (Infectious Diseases workshop, Pr. Ahd Oulad Lahsen)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Definition: > 38.3 °C, repeated, ≥ 3 weeks, no cause after initial work-up.
~25% remain undiagnosed; avoid blind antibiotics.
Four families: infections, inflammatory diseases, neoplasms, miscellaneous.
TB is the first cause in developing countries.
Inflammatory 25-30%: Horton (elderly), Still (young), lupus.
Drug fever: β-lactams, sulphonamides, methyldopa, carbamazepine.
Factitious fever: fever without tachycardia, normal tests.
History: occupation, travel, food, animals, contacts.
Admit if neutropenic, splenectomised, valvular, immunocompromised, CD4 < 200, prosthesis.
First wave: CBC, ≥ 3 blood cultures, CRP/ESR, urine, CXR, TB tests, serologies, thick smear, ultrasound.
Echocardiography is systematic in the second wave.

deeper.title: Why not simply give antibiotics
deeper.html:
Empirical antibiotics can temporarily suppress fever from a partly treated infection such as endocarditis or a deep abscess, making blood cultures negative and hiding the diagnosis for weeks. They do nothing for the many non-infectious causes and add resistance and side effects. That is why the lecture insists on a methodical work-up first.

Source: the lecture's relevance slide.

deeper.title: Why the history is the most powerful test
deeper.html:
With hundreds of possible causes, no test panel can cover them all. A single detail, such as drinking raw milk, working in sewers or a recent trip, can point straight to brucellosis, leptospirosis or malaria and spare invasive investigations. The lecture's second wave is reserved for patients in whom history and examination give no lead.

Source: the lecture's interview slides.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Rabies: viral zoonosis, always fatal once declared.
No curative treatment; prevention only.
Transmission by saliva: bites, scratches, licks on broken skin/mucosa.
Human-to-human: corneal transplant.
Morocco: dogs 89%, cats 5%; young, male, rural.
Virus travels along peripheral nerves to the CNS.
Incubation 20-60 days (15 d-1 year); shorter in children and head bites.
Prodrome: tingling at the bite site.
Furious rabies: hydrophobia, aerophobia, agitation, clear consciousness.
Death within 3-6 days.
Post-exposure: wash the wound, vaccine ± immunoglobulins.
Observe the dog (virus shed ~3 days before signs).

deeper.title: Why rabies can be prevented after the bite
deeper.html:
The virus travels slowly along nerves, taking weeks to reach the brain. A vaccine given right after exposure produces neutralising antibodies within that time, and immunoglobulins injected into the wound neutralise virus at the site immediately. Once the virus reaches the brain and symptoms appear, nothing stops it, which is why the response must be immediate.

Source: the lecture's incubation and prophylaxis slides.

deeper.title: Why washing the wound matters so much
deeper.html:
Soap and water physically remove and inactivate much of the virus before it enters nerve endings. It costs nothing, needs no centre and remains useful even if the patient arrives hours or days later, which is why the lecture calls it the simplest and most useful act.

Source: the lecture's measures in case of exposure slide.

figure.caption: From the bite to fatal encephalitis, and the window for prevention. Schematic drawn for this site.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Agent: Rickettsia conorii; vector and reservoir: Rhipicephalus sanguineus (dog tick).
Summer disease: July-September in Morocco.
Painless bite; tick must feed ≥ 20 h.
Triad: fever 39.5 °C + maculopapular rash + black eschar.
Black eschar (tache noire) in 80%: pathognomonic.
Complicated 6-7%; risk: > 60 y, diabetes, alcohol, G6PD deficiency.
Diagnosis is clinical first; IFA ≥ 1/128 or rising titres.
Doxycycline 200 mg/day for 5-7 days.
Josamycin for children and pregnant women.
Prevention: repellent, remove ticks early, control dogs.

deeper.title: Why doxycycline and not a β-lactam
deeper.html:
Rickettsiae live and multiply inside the host's endothelial cells. β-lactams barely enter cells, whereas tetracyclines such as doxycycline concentrate intracellularly and block bacterial protein synthesis. That intracellular life, which also causes the vasculitis behind the rash and the complications, is why doxycycline is the treatment.

Source: the lecture's treatment slide and the principles of antibiotic therapy.

deeper.title: Why the eschar is so valuable
deeper.html:
Serology takes days to become positive, but the black eschar marks the exact point where the tick injected the bacteria. Finding it with fever and rash in summer, especially in someone with a dog, makes the diagnosis at the bedside and allows immediate treatment; it is also the best site for a biopsy.

Source: the lecture's clinical and diagnostic slides.

figure.caption: Tick, dog and the diagnostic triad. Schematic drawn for this site.

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: TIAC: ≥ 2 grouped cases, similar (digestive) symptoms, same food; notifiable.
Mostly bacterial.
S. aureus: 2-4 h, vomiting, no fever (dairy, dishes made the day before).
C. perfringens: isolated afebrile diarrhoea (collective catering, poor refrigeration).
Salmonella: 12-24 h, febrile diarrhoea (eggs, poultry).
Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia: 48-72 h, febrile.
Rehydration first; avoid antidiarrhoeal transit slowers in invasive diarrhoea.
Antibiotics only if > 48-72 h, salmonella, dysentery, cholera or risk factors.
Collective: report, investigate, remove food, test kitchen staff.
Prevention: hands, no cooked-raw contact, < 2 h out of fridge, fridge < 4.5 °C.

deeper.title: Why a short incubation and no fever mean a toxin
deeper.html:
When bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus grow in food left at room temperature, they release heat-stable toxins into it. Eating the food delivers the toxin directly, so vomiting starts within a few hours, and since no infection is established there is no fever. Invasive bacteria like Salmonella must first multiply and invade the gut wall, which takes longer and causes fever.

Source: the lecture's pathogen table.

deeper.title: Why dishes prepared the day before are risky
deeper.html:
Cooking kills most bacteria but not the spores of Clostridium perfringens or Bacillus cereus. If a large dish cools slowly and sits out, the spores germinate and multiply, producing toxin, and reheating may not destroy it. That is why collective catering and leftovers appear again and again in TIAC investigations.

Source: the lecture's pathogen and prevention slides.

figure.caption: Incubation and fever point to the culprit. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: < 12 h, no fever: toxins (S. aureus 2-4 h, B. cereus)
> 12 h, fever: Salmonella 12-24 h; Campylobacter, Shigella 48-72 h
